content: Intestinal parasites are organisms that inhabit the gastrointestinal tract. In humans, these parasites are frequently transmitted through inadequate hygiene practices involving fecal matter, contact with animals, or consumption of undercooked or contaminated food containing parasites. The primary categories of intestinal parasites include protozoans, which are single-celled organisms, and parasitic worms, also known as helminths. Among these, protozoans such as Cryptosporidium, Microsporidia, and Isospora are particularly prevalent in individuals infected with HIV. These parasites can infect the digestive system, and it is not uncommon for multiple parasites to cause concurrent infections. Parasites can enter the intestinal tract through various routes. They may be ingested via uncooked or unwashed food, contaminated water, or unclean hands. Additionally, skin contact with soil containing larval forms of parasites can lead to infection. Certain behaviors, such as oral sex or anal-oral contact, may also facilitate transmission. Once these organisms are swallowed, they migrate to the intestines, where they can reproduce and induce disease. In some individuals, intestinal parasites may not produce any noticeable symptoms, or the symptoms may be intermittent. Common clinical manifestations include coughing, cramping abdominal pain, bloating, excessive gas, and diarrhea. In more severe cases, symptoms may include reduced libido, skin itching, fever, nausea, vomiting, or the presence of blood in the stool. Certain parasites can also lead to anemia by causing a reduction in red blood cell count. Some parasites have the ability to migrate between the lungs and the intestines, or even to other parts of the body. It is important to note that many other medical conditions can present with similar symptoms. Therefore, laboratory testing is essential to accurately identify the underlying cause. In children, parents often report symptoms such as irritability and restlessness, which may be indicative of a parasitic infection.
